nameStory: This beetle gets its "flower longhorn" name from its habit of visiting flowers to feed on pollen and nectar, combined with the characteristically long antennae that give all longhorn beetles their common name. The genus name Strangalepta comes from Greek roots meaning "twisted" or "twisted scale," though the exact reason for this name remains a bit of a mystery to beetle enthusiasts.
description: The Strangalepta Flower Longhorn Beetle is a medium-sized beetle that you'll often spot on wildflowers during summer days. Like all longhorn beetles, it has notably long antennae that can be as long as or longer than its body. This species is special because it's the only member of its genus, making it a unique find in the beetle world. Adults are active flower visitors, using their strong mandibles to feed on pollen while helping with pollination.

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are at least as long as the body, often longer, with distinct segments that feel firm when gently touched

idTips.label: Flower feeding behavior
idTips.description: Often found with head buried deep in flower centers, especially on composite flowers like goldenrod and asters

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Elongated, somewhat flattened body with a slightly narrowed waist between thorax and abdomen

idTips.label: Size range
idTips.description: Medium-sized longhorn beetle, roughly the length of a paperclip, with a solid feel when handled

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: Moves deliberately and somewhat clumsily on flowers, often tumbling when disturbed but quick to right itself

habitat: Look for this beetle in sunny meadows, field edges, and garden borders where wildflowers bloom abundantly. They're particularly fond of areas with goldenrod, asters, and other late-summer composite flowers. You'll find them from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England's diverse landscapes.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet active. Look for last year's exit holes in dead wood where larvae developed.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults emerge and can be found feeding on flowers, especially during warm, sunny days from mid-July through August.
seasonality.fall: Late-emerging adults may still be found on fall-blooming flowers like asters, but activity decreases as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity. Larvae are developing inside dead wood, preparing for next year's emergence.

funFact: This beetle is essentially a living fossil in the insect world — it's the sole survivor of its entire genus, making every individual you spot a representative of an evolutionary line that has no close relatives anywhere on Earth.
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other flower-visiting longhorn beetles, but remember that most longhorns you see on flowers in late summer are likely this species. Look for the characteristic deliberate movement and tendency to completely bury their head in flower centers, unlike other longhorns that feed more delicately.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a "longhorn" beetle, these insects are completely unrelated to longhorn cattle — the name simply refers to their impressively long antennae that can sense chemical signals from potential mates and food sources from remarkable distances.
compareHints: Since this is the only species in its genus Strangalepta, it's truly one of a kind among longhorn beetles. Compared to other flower-visiting longhorns in the family, it tends to be more persistent on individual flowers and less likely to fly away immediately when approached. Its body proportions and antenna length also tend to be more balanced than some of the more extreme longhorn species.
